Content:
To disprove a statement means to show that it is false. In this lesson, we will learn how to disprove universal statements.

Content:
Suppose we wish to disprove a universal statement of the form

Content:
[MATH: \forall x \in U, \: P(x),]

Content:
where [MATH: U] is some universal set. To do that, we must demonstrate that the statement's negation is true.

Content:
The negation of this statement is

Content:
[MATH: \neg \big( \forall x \in U, \: P(x) \big) \: \equiv \: \exists x \in U, \: \lnot P(x).]

Content:
Therefore, to disprove a universal statement, finding one value of the variable that makes the negation true is sufficient. This value is called a counterexample to the original statement.

Content:
For example, suppose we wish to disprove the following statement:

Content:
> [MATH: 5n-1] is odd for any [MATH: n \in \mathbb{Z}.]

Content:
Our statement can be written using formal notation as follows:
[MATH: 5n − 1]
We want to disprove this statement. In other words, we must show that its negation is true:
[MATH: 5n − 1]
So, we begin as follows:

Content:
> To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. In other words, we need to show that there exists an integer [MATH: n] such that [MATH: 5n-1] is even.

Content:
Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting [MATH: n=1] suffices:

Content:
> Notice that by substituting [MATH: n=1] into the expression, we obtain
> [MATH: 5n − 1|= 5(1) − 1; = 4]
> which is even.

Content:
Finally, we state our conclusion:

Content:
> So, [MATH: n=1] is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false.

sections.normalized_html:
Disprove the following statement:

[MATH: 2 \mid n^2-3] for any [MATH: n \in \mathbb{Z}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Our statement can be written as [MATH: \forall n \in \mathbb{Z}, \: 2 \mid n^2-3.] We want to disprove this statement. In other words, we must show that its negation is true: [MATH: \neg \big( \forall n \in \mathbb{Z}, \: 2 \mid n^2-3\big) \: \equiv \: \exists n \in \mathbb{Z}, \: 2 \not\mid n^2-3] So, we begin as follows:

To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. In other words, we need to show that there exists an integer [MATH: n] such that [MATH: 2 \not\mid n^2-3.]

Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting [MATH: n=0] suffices:

Notice that by substituting [MATH: n=0] into the expression, we obtain [MATH: n^{2} − 3|= (0)^{2} − 3; = − 3] which is not divisible by [MATH: 2.]

Finally, we state our conclusion:

So, [MATH: n=0] is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
To disprove a statement means to show that it is false. In this lesson, we will learn how to disprove universal statements.

Content:
Suppose we wish to disprove a universal statement of the form

Content:
[MATH: \forall x \in U, \: P(x),]

Content:
where [MATH: U] is some universal set. To do that, we must demonstrate that the statement's negation is true.

Content:
The negation of this statement is

Content:
[MATH: \neg \big( \forall x \in U, \: P(x) \big) \: \equiv \: \exists x \in U, \: \lnot P(x).]

Content:
Therefore, to disprove a universal statement, finding one value of the variable that makes the negation true is sufficient. This value is called a counterexample to the original statement.

---

Content:

[MATH: 5n − 1]
We want to disprove this statement. In other words, we must show that its negation is true:
[MATH: 5n − 1]
So, we begin as follows:

Content:
> To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. In other words, we need to show that there exists an integer [MATH: n] such that [MATH: 5n-1] is even.

Content:
Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting [MATH: n=1] suffices:

Content:
> Notice that by substituting [MATH: n=1] into the expression, we obtain
> [MATH: 5n − 1|= 5(1) − 1; = 4]
> which is even.

Content:

> So, [MATH: n=0] is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false.
